edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SPORT + SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
edition.deck: Israel’s election remains unresolved as the country’s political blocs face weeks of coalition talks. In the UK, the chancellor prepares a Budget against cost pressures, while new scrutiny falls on AI, public spending and patient safety.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise the overnight election picture and developments with immediate public significance. Treat projected results and Budget measures as provisional where the reporting does. Avoid repeating older stories without a fresh development.

content.headline: Israel’s election produces no clear winner, with Arab parties in a pivotal role
content.shortHeadline: Israel’s election leaves both blocs short of a majority
content.standfirst: Revised exit polls leave Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition tied or close, with neither near the 61 seats needed for a majority. Arab parties are projected to gain ground as coalition talks loom.

image.caption: Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot both claimed victory after the exit polls.

sources.originalTitle: Israeli exit polls suggest no clear winner in pivotal general election
Israel election too close to call as exit polls give Netanyahu bloc slightly fewer seats
Israel election: what we know so far
Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

segments.body: Exit polls from Israel’s general election show no clear path to a majority for either Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc or the opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Revised projections from broadcasters put the blocs around 51 seats apiece in the 120-seat Knesset; official results are still being counted.

segments.title: Coalition arithmetic
segments.body: The Arab parties are projected to win 18 or 19 seats, up from 10, potentially making them decisive in negotiations. Eisenkot has ruled out relying on them before the vote, while the fragmented results could leave Netanyahu’s coalition in a caretaker role as parties try to assemble a government. Absentee ballots, including many cast by military personnel, are not expected to be fully counted until Thursday.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis argues that the opposition may have to choose between negotiating with Arab-Israeli parties and giving Netanyahu a possible route back to power. Any deal would face difficult conditions and disagreement within the opposition.

segments.body: The vote was Israel’s first since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed. Campaign issues included accountability for the security failures, military-service obligations, judicial reform and Israel’s international standing. The final result and the eventual shape of a government remain uncertain.

content.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in the US after Brazil cancels his passports
content.shortHeadline: Flávio Bolsonaro reported in US after passport order
content.standfirst: The defeated Brazilian presidential candidate is reported to have reached the United States after missing a court-ordered deadline to surrender his passports. He has not been charged in the money-laundering investigation and denies wrongdoing.

image.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro speaks to the media in Rio de Janeiro.

sources.originalTitle: Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in US after Brazil cancels his passports
Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say

segments.body: Flávio Bolsonaro has arrived in the United States, sources told the BBC, hours after Brazil cancelled his passports because he missed a deadline to hand them over. The Supreme Court order was made as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering; Bolsonaro has not been charged and denies the allegations.

The BBC reports that Bolsonaro met his brother Eduardo in Florida, but says his route from Brazil is unclear. His lawyers said they did not know what had happened, and neither brother was directly available for comment. A senior US official said visas would be issued to Bolsonaro and his family.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva called the reported departure shameful, according to the Guardian, while Bolsonaro has not conceded defeat and has challenged the election result. The BBC says he is also under investigation in a separate inquiry; his intentions in the US remain unknown.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports Lula’s criticism of Bolsonaro’s apparent departure and describes political uncertainty over who might lead Brazil’s right after the election. The report also notes that accounts of Bolsonaro’s route varied before the BBC confirmed his reported arrival.

content.headline: India-China thaw faces new doubts after border official’s account
content.shortHeadline: Indian official’s claims unsettle China border thaw
content.standfirst: An Indian border police chief says Chinese troops returned to disputed areas in Arunachal Pradesh and pitched tents inside territory claimed by India. Delhi has not explicitly denied his account; Beijing says its patrols follow agreements.

image.caption: India and China have been cautiously rebuilding relations since their 2020 border clashes.

sources.originalTitle: India and China were easing tensions - then a border official spoke out

segments.body: India’s border police chief, Shatrujeet Singh Kapur, said Chinese troops returned in larger numbers to disputed areas of Arunachal Pradesh this year and pitched tents six to seven kilometres inside what India considers its side of the Line of Actual Control. His public remarks have triggered a political dispute in Delhi.

segments.title: A fragile improvement
segments.body: The claims come after India and China took steps to ease tensions following deadly clashes in 2020, including restoring direct flights and easing visa restrictions. India’s government has not explicitly denied Kapur’s account. A foreign ministry spokesman said the border situation is sometimes disturbed when Chinese forces depart from established patrol patterns.

China’s foreign ministry said it had consistently followed agreements and described its activity as normal patrols to safeguard its territorial sovereignty. The disputed frontier remains undemarcated in many places, and analysts cited by the BBC say improved diplomatic ties do not necessarily mean greater stability on the ground.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s reporting connects the border dispute to a wider economic relationship: bilateral trade reached $151bn last year, with India dependent on Chinese imports for goods including machinery, batteries and rare-earth magnets.

content.headline: King Charles acknowledges slavery’s legacy as Caribbean tour begins
content.shortHeadline: King acknowledges slavery’s legacy on Caribbean tour
content.standfirst: Charles says Commonwealth leaders will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit next week, as Caribbean nations renew calls for an apology and reparations. The Bahamas National Reparations Committee says his remarks do not go far enough.

image.caption: King Charles with Bahamas Prime Minister Philip Davis as his Caribbean tour begins.

sources.originalTitle: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit

segments.body: King Charles began a nine-day Caribbean tour in the Bahamas, where he acknowledged “the great suffering of the past” and said parts of Bahamian culture were “born out of darkness”. He confirmed that Commonwealth leaders will discuss slavery’s legacy at their meeting in Antigua and Barbuda next week.

segments.title: Calls for more than recognition
segments.body: The Bahamas National Reparations Committee said the King’s words fell short of what justice requires, calling for a full formal apology and action to address harms committed in the Crown’s name. Its chair, Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, described the remarks as hollow platitudes, while the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission has called for remorse.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that reparations advocates welcomed the acknowledgement of suffering but say it does not address the Crown’s role or meet their demands for apology and reparative action.

segments.body: The tour also includes Guyana and will culminate at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting. Buckingham Palace says the programme will focus mainly on modern partnerships while reflecting the King’s longstanding interest in the region’s history. In line with the UK government’s position, he will not offer an apology or reparations.

content.headline: Egypt court fines Lina Attalah and orders independent news site to close
content.shortHeadline: Egypt court fines editor and orders Mada Masr closure
content.standfirst: Mada Masr editor Lina Attalah was detained for several hours after a court imposed the maximum fine and ordered the outlet closed. The ruling draws condemnation from press-freedom groups; her lawyers are challenging a separate sentence issued in absentia.

image.caption: Mada Masr editor Lina Attalah, whose outlet was ordered closed by an Egyptian court.

sources.originalTitle: Egypt court fines journalist Lina Attalah and orders news site's closure

segments.body: A court in Egypt fined Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of independent outlet Mada Masr, 3m Egyptian pounds and ordered the website closed, her lawyers and the outlet say. Attalah was detained for several hours and released after the fine was paid. She rejected the charge of managing an unlicensed website.

segments.title: A wider press-freedom concern
segments.body: Amnesty International called the verdict a “crushing blow to press freedom”; the Committee to Protect Journalists described Mada Masr as an important source of critical reporting. The outlet says it had sought a licence since Egypt’s 2018 media law, but its applications were rejected or left unanswered.

perspectives.body: Mada Masr’s lawyer alleges the judge excluded most observers, rejected defence requests and appointed a lawyer over Attalah’s objection. These accounts are attributed to the lawyer and the outlet.

segments.body: Attalah’s lawyers have also begun challenging a one-year prison sentence issued in absentia in 2024, with a retrial hearing scheduled for 11 November. Amnesty says Attalah has faced years of harassment and investigations linked to the outlet’s reporting.

content.headline: AI’s promise in science meets concerns over accuracy and trust
content.shortHeadline: AI science advances raise questions about trust
content.standfirst: AI has helped researchers make major discoveries, but disputed claims, invented citations and AI-written research are testing scientific safeguards. Researchers and publishers are working out how to verify results and keep humans accountable.

sources.originalTitle: A bust-up between mathematicians is fuelling fears that AI could undermine science

segments.body: Artificial intelligence has accelerated some scientific work, including the prediction of protein structures, but its growing role has raised concerns about the reliability and novelty of research. A dispute over an OpenAI claim to have solved a major mathematical problem highlights questions that remain unresolved about how the work was produced.

segments.title: Verification under pressure
segments.body: Researchers cited by the BBC warn that AI-generated material can include fabricated references and distort peer review. One study found nearly 90% of more than a million biomedical papers it examined carried possible AI-writing fingerprints by late 2025, though AI detection tools are imperfect. Other researchers have questioned whether some AI-generated materials discoveries were as novel as claimed.

Publishers are developing screening systems and rules for handling AI, while scientists who support its use argue that people must understand and take responsibility for what an AI agent produces. The reporting also describes successful research assisted by AI, underscoring that the issue is how to validate its contribution, not simply whether to use it.

content.headline: China’s elderly now outnumber children in the dependent population
content.shortHeadline: China’s ageing population passes a demographic milestone
content.standfirst: Official figures show China’s elderly dependency ratio reached 23% last year, above the 22% figure for children. The shift adds pressure to pensions, healthcare and families, though experts caution that dependency ratios do not capture older people’s full contribution.

sources.originalTitle: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids

segments.body: China’s government says the ratio of people aged 65 and older to the working-age population reached 23% last year, overtaking the child dependency ratio of 22%. The country has more than 223 million people aged 65 and above and about 213 million children aged 14 and under.

Analysts say the demographic shift could increase demands on pensions, healthcare and long-term care, while affecting the workforce and economic growth. China has eased restrictions on family size and introduced support for older people, but birth rates remain low amid factors including living costs and changing social roles.

The dependency ratio is widely used but has limits: it does not account for improvements in health or the agency of older people, one expert told the BBC. Some older Chinese people also enter later life with higher incomes and stronger purchasing power than previous generations.

content.headline: Luxury cruise ship suspends voyage, leaving passengers in Cambodia
content.shortHeadline: Cruise ship suspends world voyage amid fuel costs
content.standfirst: The operator of Villa Vie Odyssey says soaring fuel costs have forced it to suspend operations and is working with passengers on disembarkation and temporary accommodation. It says a 60-day restructuring effort has no guaranteed outcome.

image.caption: Villa Vie Odyssey, whose round-the-world voyage has been suspended in Cambodia.

sources.originalTitle: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs

segments.body: Villa Vie Odyssey, more than 750 days into a planned years-long voyage around the world, has suspended operations in Cambodia. Its US-based operator says it is arranging for passengers to disembark and finding temporary living arrangements; around 200 people were reportedly aboard.

segments.title: Costs overwhelm the itinerary
segments.body: The company says fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia have climbed to as much as $8,000 a month from $1,800. Slowing the itinerary and spending longer in port were not enough to offset the increase, and passing the full cost on to residents was not considered realistic.

The operator plans to spend the next 60 days on restructuring and recapitalisation but says no outcome is assured. The ship had set out from Belfast in October 2024 on a voyage planned to cover nearly 150 countries.

content.headline: UK Budget expected to ease household costs as fiscal room remains tight
content.shortHeadline: Budget faces cost pressures and limited room to spend
content.standfirst: Chancellor John Healey is expected to offer temporary help with household costs and announce longer-term energy reforms, while limiting major tax and spending decisions. Rising borrowing costs and uncertain forecasts leave little room for manoeuvre.

image.caption: The chancellor faces choices over household support, growth and the public finances.

sources.originalTitle: Chancellor targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’
Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellor

segments.body: Chancellor John Healey is due to deliver his first Budget on Wednesday, with the government promising some “breathing space” as higher energy costs and inflation put pressure on families, businesses and public finances. The measures are expected to be modest, with important tax and spending decisions deferred.

segments.title: A narrow fiscal buffer
segments.body: The Resolution Foundation estimates the headroom against the government’s fiscal rules may have fallen from £23.6bn to about £12bn as borrowing costs rise. Investors are watching how much room Healey retains for further shocks. The estimates remain dependent on the Office for Budget Responsibility’s assessment of inflation, employment, pay and growth.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s chart-led analysis highlights the tension between retaining enough fiscal headroom to reassure bond investors and funding household support, defence and regional growth.

segments.title: Measures under consideration
segments.body: Expected measures include temporary help for poorer households before energy bills rise in January, changes to the carers’ allowance earnings limit and a planned fuel-duty increase being cancelled. The government is also expected to set out energy-market reforms and a roadmap for devolving some tax revenues to local leaders; the details have not yet been confirmed.

content.headline: MPs warn Sizewell C deal could leave taxpayers and billpayers exposed
content.shortHeadline: Watchdog warns of major risks in Sizewell C funding
content.standfirst: The Public Accounts Committee says the nuclear project could cost up to £47.7bn, with taxpayers and energy customers bearing substantial risks if costs rise. The government disputes the committee’s assessment and says the deal incentivises investors to control costs.

image.caption: Sizewell C is expected to cost between £40.5bn and £47.7bn.

sources.originalTitle: Plan for multibillion-pound Sizewell nuclear plant a ‘terrible deal’ for UK taxpayers, MPs say

segments.body: The Public Accounts Committee says the funding model for Sizewell C exposes taxpayers and energy consumers to an “extraordinary” level of risk. It warns costs could approach £48bn, with the public potentially facing a further £9.8bn during construction and £12bn over the plant’s 60-year operating life.

segments.title: Who carries the risk?
segments.body: The government holds a 44.9% stake in the Suffolk project after buying out Chinese state developer CGN. The committee says the public could be called on to cover multibillion-pound overruns while private investors would need to contribute only £30m more. It has asked ministers to provide their cost scenarios and give regular progress updates.

The government says the committee overlooks investor incentives and argues Sizewell C could save £2bn a year across the energy system once operational. It expects construction to cost between £40.5bn and £47.7bn and to finish between 2039 and 2043; the committee and critics dispute whether the risks to households are justified.

perspectives.body: The Nuclear Industry Association argues that Sizewell C would provide reliable low-carbon power and reduce system costs. Campaigners who gave evidence to the committee say abandoning the project could cost less than decades of higher bills.

content.headline: AI bots made up three-quarters of responses to UK vape-ban consultation
content.shortHeadline: AI bots flooded UK consultation on disposable vapes
content.standfirst: Researchers say automated submissions tried to sway a 2023 consultation against a ban on disposable vapes. The government identified and excluded 90,835 bot responses, but experts warn that similar interference may be harder to detect next time.

image.caption: Researchers say automated responses targeted a government consultation on disposable vapes.

sources.originalTitle: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban

segments.body: A study says 90,835 of the 118,756 responses to a 2023 UK consultation on tobacco and vapes were generated by bots. The Department of Health and Social Care identified and excluded the automated submissions; nearly all opposed the proposed ban on disposable vapes.

segments.title: A test for public consultation
segments.body: Researchers describe the case as the first documented large-scale automated attempt to interfere in a formal public-health consultation. They warn that fake responses can make a handful of interests appear to represent a mass movement, while stronger screening can also make it harder for genuine participants to take part.

The department says its controls worked and that the consultation informed the ban, later passed into law. Campaigners say governments need better screening and transparency, but there is no single fix as AI-generated submissions become harder to distinguish from people’s responses.

content.headline: Former Met officer found guilty of rape and other sexual offences
content.shortHeadline: Former Met officer convicted of rape and sexual assault
content.standfirst: Mark Tyrrell, who worked in the same Met unit as Wayne Couzens, was found guilty of raping a woman and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of 13 other charges, including another rape count, and is due to be sentenced in December.

image.caption: Mark Tyrrell worked in the Metropolitan Police’s parliamentary and diplomatic protection command.

sources.originalTitle: Former Met officer who worked with Wayne Couzens found guilty of rape

segments.body: A jury at Southwark Crown Court found former Metropolitan Police officer Mark Tyrrell guilty of rape, three counts of sexual assault and perverting the course of justice. The court heard that the woman had repeatedly said no. Tyrrell said the sex was consensual.

segments.title: Police conduct under scrutiny
segments.body: Tyrrell had been attached to the Met’s parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, where convicted rapists Wayne Couzens and David Carrick also worked. He was found not guilty of 13 other charges, including one count of rape, and will be sentenced on 16 December.

The Met’s specialist operations commander said the conduct was abhorrent, particularly because Tyrrell was a serving officer who had gained the woman’s trust. Tyrrell had previously admitted misconduct in public office and a separate offence of persuading the woman to lie to police.

content.headline: Two men charged over alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford appear in court
content.shortHeadline: Two charged over alleged plot at RAF Fairford
content.standfirst: Mohmed Abdulkarim and Nouman Essghir appeared in court over alleged offences linked to the US-operated airbase. One is charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service believed by police to be Iran; Iran has denied involvement in the incident.

image.caption: Mohmed Abdulkarim and Nouman Essghir appeared in court on Tuesday.

sources.originalTitle: Two in court over alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford

segments.body: Two British men appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court in connection with an alleged plot involving RAF Fairford. Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, is charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police believe to be Iran. Nouman Essghir, also 24, is charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: The charges follow an incident near the Gloucestershire airbase in September, when three suspicious vans were reported, residents were evacuated and a cordon was put in place. Police said no explosives were found, but seized petrol. Essghir was remanded in custody; Abdulkarim was granted bail with conditions. Their case is due back at the Old Bailey on 20 November.

Police say eight men have been arrested during the counter-terror investigation. Iran has previously denied involvement. The allegations have not been tested in court, and the reasons for the police actions remain part of the investigation.

content.headline: Government-backed loans for heat pumps and solar upgrades go on sale
content.shortHeadline: Low-cost loans launched for home energy upgrades
content.standfirst: Households can apply for government-supported loans for heat pumps, solar panels and batteries, with borrowing of up to £35,000. The scheme offers a route to spread costs, but it does not cover insulation and eligibility depends on lenders’ terms.

image.caption: The loan scheme covers heat pumps, solar panels and home batteries.

sources.originalTitle: Homes across UK to get low- or no-interest loans to fund solar panels and heat pumps
Low-interest loans for heat pumps now available – how to apply

segments.body: The Warm Home Loans scheme has launched across the UK, offering households low- or no-interest borrowing for home upgrades including heat pumps, solar panels and batteries. Loans range from £7,500 to £35,000, with energy suppliers and participating lenders offering products to customers.

segments.title: What the scheme does and does not cover
segments.body: The government says a heat pump, battery and solar panels could save up to £550 a year on energy bills, potentially £300 more with a time-of-use tariff. The loans do not cover insulation, which may help a heat pump work efficiently. Citizens Advice warns that some households may be unable to borrow or afford the upfront costs.

perspectives.body: Citizens Advice says the scheme may help households able to borrow, but warns that families who earn too much for low-income support and cannot take on debt could be left out.

segments.body: The loans may be combined with grants of up to £9,000 for eligible heat-pump installations, according to the government. The launch comes as the Budget approaches and while reports say ministers are considering cuts to the Boiler Upgrade Scheme; the extent of any changes has not been confirmed.

content.headline: Venstre expels MP after he refuses to promise loyalty to party votes
content.shortHeadline: Venstre expels MP after loyalty dispute
content.standfirst: Preben Bang Henriksen will continue as an independent after Venstre’s parliamentary group voted to expel him. The dispute follows internal divisions over a fertiliser law and a party demand that members follow majority decisions.

image.caption: Preben Bang Henriksen was expelled from Venstre’s parliamentary group.

sources.originalTitle: Troels Lund: Preben Bang ville ikke være loyal over for flertallet

segments.body: Venstre has expelled MP Preben Bang Henriksen from its parliamentary group after he said he could not promise to follow the group’s decisions in future votes. Party leader Troels Lund Poulsen said members should back the majority once they leave the group room; the party did not disclose the vote count.

segments.title: A dispute over parliamentary freedom
segments.body: Bang Henriksen said he would not “deposit his vote” with a majority, arguing that doing so would conflict with the Constitution. He will remain in parliament as an independent and says he has no current plans to join another party.

The dispute follows a split over a controversial fertiliser law, which five Venstre MPs opposed in September. Four have now promised to follow the party line; Søren Gade left parliament last week amid the internal conflict. Venstre’s group now has 17 seats.

content.headline: Rigshospitalet inquiry into surgery faces challenge from national cancer doctors
content.shortHeadline: Cancer doctors defend surgery at centre of Rigshospitalet inquiry
content.standfirst: An external review will examine whether rules for recording experimental surgery were followed at Rigshospitalet. The national pancreatic cancer group says the procedure under scrutiny is established practice and patients were selected collectively.

image.caption: Three surgeons were recently dismissed from Rigshospitalet, prompting scrutiny of the department.

sources.originalTitle: Kaotiske tilstande på specialafdeling på Rigshospitalet gør patienter og pårørende nervøse: 'Det har været rigtig ubehageligt at følge med i'
Kræftlæger bakker op om fyrede kirurger på Rigshospitalet

segments.body: Rigshospitalet is facing an external review of whether scientific procedures for documenting experimental surgery were followed in past treatment. The inquiry follows the dismissal of three senior doctors and has left some patients and relatives uneasy about the department’s future.

segments.title: Doctors dispute the premise
segments.body: The Danish Pancreas Cancer Group says the operation at issue, DP-CAR, is an established treatment used at major European centres, not an experimental procedure. It says patients were selected through a joint decision by doctors from across the country and that the treatment and alternatives were explained to patients.

perspectives.body: The national group says the review’s questions reflect on pancreatic-cancer specialists across Denmark because patient selection and treatment decisions were made collectively, not by one Rigshospitalet surgeon.

segments.body: The hospital and regional authorities say the review will investigate whether guidelines were followed, but have not detailed the suspected shortcomings. A patient’s relative told DR that the recent upheaval had shaken their confidence, despite being satisfied with care during her husband’s earlier treatment.

content.headline: Nearly 20,000 Danish websites remain exposed to PHP security flaws
content.shortHeadline: Thousands of Danish websites remain vulnerable
content.standfirst: Dansk Industri says about 19,700 .dk websites have yet to install a security update after serious PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. It says many use unsupported software; no successful attacks linked to the flaws had been reported at the time of the report.

image.caption: Thousands of Danish websites have yet to address the reported PHP security flaws.

sources.originalTitle: Sikkerhedsbrud lukkede hjemmesider verden over: I Danmark er tusindvis stadig i farezonen

segments.body: Almost 20,000 Danish websites remain vulnerable after two serious flaws were found in PHP, a widely used programming language, according to Dansk Industri. The organisation says 19,700 .dk sites had not installed the security update nearly a week after the alert.

segments.title: Unsupported systems are harder to fix
segments.body: Dansk Industri estimates that as many as 17,700 of the sites run software that is no longer maintained, so installing the update will not solve the problem. The organisation says those sites need to be moved to supported software and is contacting affected members with advice.

The organisation says it had no reports of successful attacks tied to the PHP flaws at the time of publication. DR had asked the relevant Danish authorities about possible warnings or breaches but had not received a response.

content.headline: New Danish news outlet Y launches with AI, but researcher sees little new
content.shortHeadline: AI-led news outlet Y draws a cautious first review
content.standfirst: The new free outlet says AI is involved in almost every stage of production, from ideas and source selection to articles. A media researcher says its opening output relied heavily on wire copy and questions how much original journalism it adds.

image.caption: Michael Dyrby leads Y, a new Danish outlet using AI throughout much of its news production.

sources.originalTitle: Nyt AI-medie uden journalister skuffer forsker
I morgen går nyt AI-medie i luften: 'Vi går faktisk mod strømmen'

segments.body: Y, a new Danish news outlet led by former TV 2 and B.T. news director Michael Dyrby, has launched without employing journalists. Editors use AI for much of the process, including idea development, choosing sources and producing articles.

segments.title: Originality and transparency
segments.body: On launch day, media researcher Peder Hammerskov told DR that the outlet’s presentation felt heavy and its content added little new. He counted 22 of 43 articles based on Ritzau, Reuters or press releases, and 12 drawing on other outlets’ reporting. He also questioned whether readers would notice how AI was used.

perspectives.body: Hammerskov said the outlet’s first-day mix resembled a news agency and that its AI processes were not especially visible to users. He welcomed the debate about innovation but said Y must still prove it is relevant.

segments.body: Y’s stated ambition is to experiment with new angles and audio versions of stories, while editors remain responsible for what is published. The initial assessment is based on its launch-day output; whether the approach can sustain original reporting remains to be seen.

content.headline: Fleetwood knock Arsenal out of the Carabao Cup in a stunning shootout win
content.shortHeadline: Fleetwood stun Arsenal to reach Carabao Cup quarter-finals
content.standfirst: League Two Fleetwood held the Premier League champions to a 1-1 draw before winning on penalties. Arsenal’s 16-year-old Max Dowman was sent off late on, adding a further twist to a remarkable cup upset.

image.caption: Conor Haughey celebrates after scoring the penalty that sent Fleetwood into the quarter-finals.

sources.originalTitle: Dowman sees red as Arsenal dumped out, but did Arteta go too far?
'Biggest night in the club's history' for fearless Fleetwood

segments.body: Fleetwood Town have reached the Carabao Cup quarter-finals for the first time after eliminating Arsenal on penalties. Aaron Loupalo-Bi put the hosts ahead, Viktor Gyökeres equalised after the break, and the League Two side held on through normal time despite Arsenal dominating possession and attempts.

segments.title: A night to remember in Fleetwood
segments.body: Arsenal were reduced to 10 men when Dowman was sent off late in the match after reacting to a challenge. Goalkeeper Jay Lynch saved penalties from Ben White, Martin Ødegaard and Bruno Guimarães; Conor Haughey then scored the decisive kick. Fleetwood manager Matt Lawlor called it the club’s biggest night.

perspectives.body: Fleetwood left-back Jake Batty said the team’s league form had been below expectations, but cup football had brought out a different spirit. He hoped the excitement would carry into their next league game.

segments.title: Questions over Arteta’s reaction
segments.body: Manager Mikel Arteta looked angry as Dowman left the pitch and said the team had already discussed the need to control emotions. Paul Merson argued Arteta should have put an arm around the 16-year-old; former Everton midfielder Leon Osman called Dowman’s response poor and said he hoped the teenager learned from it.

content.headline: Abhishek Sharma’s 113 powers India to a record-breaking T20 chase of New Zealand
content.shortHeadline: Abhishek’s 113 leads India to a stunning T20 chase
content.standfirst: India reached 199 in just 13.2 overs in Wellington, with Abhishek Sharma making 113 from 38 balls. The six-wicket win gives India an unassailable 3-0 lead in the five-match series.

sources.originalTitle: Abhishek hits 35-ball ton as India hammer New Zealand

segments.body: Abhishek Sharma hit 113 from 38 balls as India chased New Zealand’s 198-3 in 13.2 overs to win the third T20 by six wickets. He struck nine fours and 11 sixes, with 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi contributing 45 from 19 balls in an opening stand of 133.

segments.title: Series won with two matches left
segments.body: India’s 118 runs in the powerplay set a new record for international T20s, and the result gives them a 3-0 lead in the five-match series. Daryl Mitchell had earlier made 89 from 52 balls for New Zealand, but India reached the target with 40 balls to spare.

content.headline: Manchester United keep Michael Carrick in charge for Chelsea trip
content.shortHeadline: Man Utd stick with Carrick for Chelsea trip
content.standfirst: After considering his position following successive heavy defeats, United have decided their head coach will lead the team at Chelsea. The club has set no timetable for a further decision as it tries to steady a turbulent situation.

image.caption: Michael Carrick acknowledges supporters after Manchester United’s defeat by Bournemouth.

sources.originalTitle: Man Utd stick with Carrick - inside a turbulent 48 hours at Old Trafford

segments.body: Michael Carrick will remain Manchester United head coach for Saturday’s trip to Chelsea. The decision followed discussions at the club after defeats by Como and Bournemouth, with United 16th in the table. Carrick had said after the Bournemouth loss that he was carrying on as normal, without assuming what would happen next.

segments.title: No timetable for what comes next
segments.body: United have not set a deadline for reviewing Carrick’s position. The report says senior figures also believe the players must take responsibility for underperforming, while the club’s leadership has faced scrutiny. A decision after the international break is described as an obvious point to reassess, not a confirmed plan.

content.headline: England eliminated from ODI tri-series after Sri Lanka beat Pakistan
content.shortHeadline: England out of ODI tri-series after Sri Lanka win
content.standfirst: Sri Lanka’s eight-wicket victory in Lahore ended England’s hopes of reaching Saturday’s final. England have lost all three matches and will play Sri Lanka on Thursday in a match that can no longer affect qualification.

sources.originalTitle: England out of tri-series after Sri Lanka beat Pakistan

segments.body: England are out of the 50-over tri-series in Pakistan after Sri Lanka bowled the hosts out for 110 and chased the target in 18.1 overs. England needed Pakistan to win to keep their own route to Saturday’s final open; Sri Lanka’s eight-wicket victory closed it.

segments.title: A setback after a stronger year
segments.body: The exit follows three defeats, including losses after England were well placed chasing 303 and after failing to defend 430 against Sri Lanka. England had built momentum with ODI wins earlier in 2026, making this tournament a setback ahead of their scheduled Australia tour in November.

content.headline: Stuart Broad calls Lancashire’s treatment of James Anderson ‘disrespectful’
content.shortHeadline: Broad criticises Lancashire over Anderson decision
content.standfirst: Broad says Lancashire should have given Anderson a better send-off after deciding not to renew his contract. Anderson has not announced his retirement, and other counties are understood to be interested.

image.caption: Stuart Broad and James Anderson, England’s long-time bowling partners.

sources.originalTitle: Lancs treatment of Anderson 'disrespectful' - Broad

segments.body: Stuart Broad has criticised Lancashire’s handling of James Anderson’s departure, calling it “pretty disrespectful” and saying the county should have given the England great a better send-off. Lancashire has decided not to renew Anderson’s contract after he took 50 County Championship wickets last season.

segments.title: Anderson’s next step is unclear
segments.body: Broad said he believed Anderson still had a great deal to offer and that counties had already made contact. Anderson has expressed sadness at Lancashire’s decision but has not announced his retirement; Lancashire has said it will look into arranging a farewell.

content.headline: Starc’s late burst lifts Australia after Cummins chooses to bowl
content.shortHeadline: Starc’s late burst lifts Australia in Cape Town decider
content.standfirst: Australia dismissed South Africa for 329 on the first day of the series decider after a difficult opening session. Mitchell Starc took six wickets, including four in the closing overs, but the result remains undecided.

sources.originalTitle: Australia fight back to keep Cummins out of unwanted club... for now

segments.body: Australia fought back to bowl South Africa out for 329 on day one in Cape Town. After South Africa reached 203-1, Australia took regular wickets in the afternoon, then Mitchell Starc struck four times in the late spell to finish with 6-72.

segments.title: The toss decision remains in focus
segments.body: Pat Cummins chose to bowl after winning the toss, saying there was moisture in the pitch. The report notes that South Africa made 140 in the first session and that the late recovery does not, by itself, prove the decision was right. Australia’s batting response and the match outcome are still to come.

content.headline: Derek McInnes says he feels ‘guilt’ over leaving Hearts for Rangers
content.shortHeadline: McInnes accepts Hearts fans’ anger over Rangers move
content.standfirst: The Rangers manager is preparing to return to Tynecastle for the first time since leaving Hearts in the summer. He understands why supporters may react badly, despite his pride in what he achieved in Edinburgh.

image.caption: Derek McInnes, who is returning to Tynecastle as Rangers manager.

sources.originalTitle: McInnes admits 'guilt' over Hearts exit for Rangers

segments.body: Derek McInnes says he feels “guilt” about leaving Hearts for Rangers and accepts he may receive a hostile reception when he returns to Tynecastle. Hearts came close to winning the title under him last season, losing to Celtic on the final day.

segments.title: Pride in his time at Hearts
segments.body: McInnes said he loved his time at Hearts and was proud of what the team achieved, but understood supporters could feel let down by his move to Ibrox. He also described Hearts as title contenders under their new head coach, Wouter Vrancken.

content.headline: David Bowie’s lost 1978 concert film is heading to arenas in 2027
content.shortHeadline: Bowie’s lost 1978 concert film is heading to arenas
content.standfirst: Director Brett Morgen spent years restoring footage of two Earl’s Court shows. The result will be presented as a multimedia arena event, with Bowie’s 1978 performance framed for a 2027 audience.

image.caption: David Bowie performing at Earl’s Court during the 1978 Isolar II tour.

sources.originalTitle: ‘How on earth is this man not sweating?’ The director who spent 10 years painstakingly remastering Bowie’s ‘greatest filmed performance’
‘Lost’ 1978 David Bowie tour film to play arenas in 2027, remastered by Moonage Daydream director Brett Morgen

segments.body: In 1978, David Bowie commissioned director David Hemmings to film two Earl’s Court concerts. The footage was never released, and Bowie later said he disliked how it had been shot. Brett Morgen discovered the 35mm film while working on his Bowie documentary, Moonage Daydream, and has spent years restoring it.

segments.title: From archive to arena
segments.body: The 2027 presentation, titled Stage, will use multiple screens, lighting and immersive sound rather than simply showing a concert film in a cinema. The shows capture Bowie and his band on the Isolar II tour, performing material from Low and “Heroes” alongside older songs. The project is due to premiere at the Berlin film festival in February before touring.

content.headline: Macklemore’s Dublin benefit show turns a tour into a collective statement
content.shortHeadline: Macklemore’s Dublin benefit show becomes a collective statement
content.standfirst: The first European date of the rapper’s Free Palestine tour brought together Hozier, Kneecap and other guests at a sold-out 3Arena. The review finds a show whose scale and purpose made it feel like more than a concert.

image.caption: Macklemore performing in Dublin on the Free Palestine tour.

sources.originalTitle: Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour review – a triumph of a show with performances from Hozier, Kneecap and more

segments.body: Macklemore’s sold-out Dublin show brought together local and international performers, activists and video-message guests, with proceeds from the tour going to organisations assisting Palestinians. Hozier, Kneecap, Beoga and Palestinian American DJ Habibeats were among those appearing, alongside messages from actors and musicians.

segments.title: The cause and the show
segments.body: The review describes a crowd with an “infectiously giddy excitement” and a bill that moved between music, advocacy and speeches. Kneecap’s chaotic set and Hozier’s audience-facing performance stood out; when Macklemore finally took the stage, the critic heard a renewed sense of purpose in his older hits as well as his newer material.

content.headline: Jack Antonoff stands by the love songs he wrote before his marriage ended
content.shortHeadline: Jack Antonoff stands by songs written before his marriage ended
content.standfirst: The Bleachers frontman says performing songs about his marriage after its breakdown has become a way to honour what he felt at the time. He also speaks candidly about grief, online criticism and the costs of touring.

image.caption: Jack Antonoff, second from right, with his band Bleachers.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’d rather live through something publicly than escape it privately’: Jack Antonoff on survivor’s guilt and still singing love songs after his breakup

segments.body: Jack Antonoff decided not to change Bleachers’ setlist after his marriage ended, even though it includes songs written about that relationship. He says the choice reflects the honesty he owes his audience: he does not want to rewrite the past, and has found that singing the material can be meaningful for both him and listeners.

segments.title: An unusually candid pop career
segments.body: The interview also explores the tension between Antonoff’s confessional work with Bleachers and his role as a producer for major pop stars. He discusses the death of his sister and what he calls survivor’s guilt, criticises the experience of buying concert tickets through Live Nation, and says he feels emboldened to speak in support of Palestine at shows.

content.headline: Manic Street Preachers revisit the weight of The Holy Bible and Richey Edwards
content.shortHeadline: Manic Street Preachers face the legacy of The Holy Bible
content.standfirst: James Dean Bradfield reflects on performing the band’s 1994 album in full, its difficult lyrics and the disappearance of lyricist Richey Edwards. A newly released live recording preserves the group’s attempt to meet their past directly.

image.caption: James Dean Bradfield, Nicky Wire and Sean Moore of Manic Street Preachers.

sources.originalTitle: Manic Street Preachers: ‘We just weren’t equipped to deal with Richey’s problems’

segments.body: Manic Street Preachers’ new live album captures their 2014 performances of The Holy Bible, the dark and politically confrontational record whose lyrics were chiefly written by Richey Edwards. Edwards disappeared in 1995 and was legally declared dead in 2008. For Bradfield, revisiting the songs meant confronting their language and the absence that has shaped the band ever since.

segments.title: What the songs still ask
segments.body: Bradfield says the album is not simply a collection of horrors: some songs show empathy for people living with eating disorders and the victims of war. He also recalls how the band, young and unequipped to respond to Edwards’s deteriorating mental health, now wonders whether they should have stopped him touring. The anniversary performances were difficult, he says, but the band felt they had done the record justice.

content.headline: Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show he helped produce
content.shortHeadline: Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show
content.standfirst: After years of helping Roc Nation produce the NFL’s halftime entertainment, the rapper will take the stage himself at Super Bowl LXI in California. The announcement follows a recent run of concerts at the same stadium.

image.caption: Jay-Z performing in Paris.

sources.originalTitle: Jay-Z picks headliner for 2027 Super Bowl half-time show … Jay-Z

segments.body: Jay-Z has been named the featured performer at the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show, scheduled for 14 February at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. His company Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL on entertainment production since 2019. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said he had hoped Jay-Z would perform one day.

The announcement marks a change from Jay-Z’s earlier reluctance to perform at the event: when Roc Nation began working with the NFL, he said that if the agreement was about him taking the stage, the conversation could end. The 56-year-old has not released a solo album since 2017, but the report notes his extensive catalogue and recent concerts at SoFi Stadium.

content.headline: Neil Young sues Trump’s political action committee again over his song
content.shortHeadline: Neil Young sues Trump’s PAC over “Rockin’ in the Free World”
content.standfirst: Young is seeking $10 million in a new copyright lawsuit over the song’s use at Donald Trump’s rallies. The filing says a 2020 settlement promised the track would not be used again without permission.

image.caption: Neil Young in 2019.

sources.originalTitle: Neil Young files second lawsuit against Trump for unauthorised use of Rockin’ in the Free World at rallies

segments.body: Neil Young has filed a second lawsuit over the use of “Rockin’ in the Free World” at Donald Trump’s political rallies, this time naming the Trump 47 Committee. The suit, filed in federal court in Virginia, seeks $10 million in reputational damages and an injunction against further public performances.

segments.title: A dispute that has returned
segments.body: Young’s first case, filed in 2020 against another Trump organisation, was settled. The new suit says that organisation promised not to use the song again without a licence and permission. It cites the song’s use at an Ohio rally on 12 October and alleges it was played at other rallies. The Trump administration had not responded to the suit at the time of the report.

content.headline: Caroline Rose turns suburban oddballs into punk-fuelled comedy
content.shortHeadline: Caroline Rose’s new album makes room for suburban oddballs
content.standfirst: On their seventh album, the singer-songwriter embraces the anarchic, funny side of their writing, pairing fast, distorted songs with portraits of misfits and strained lives. The review hears a record that is both gleefully absurd and unexpectedly tender.

sources.originalTitle: Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall

segments.body: Caroline Rose’s Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall returns to “Yip Yip Yow,” a song they first performed in 2015 and later released as a single. The new version is louder and rougher, setting the tone for an album that trades the melancholy of their previous record for gutter-punk guitars, speed and a deliberately unruly sense of humour.

segments.title: Funny, but not weightless
segments.body: The review finds Rose’s cartoonish cast of suburban outsiders funny without making their troubles disposable. “Conversation with Shiv” looks back on a friendship marked by drug use and money problems, while the album’s title reflects Rose’s bemusement at a shopping centre named for the queer poet Walt Whitman. Under the jokes, the critic hears a portrait of people living at the margins of a capitalist society.

content.headline: Tony Iommi finds a forceful new voice for his return to solo metal
content.shortHeadline: Tony Iommi’s return to solo work goes back to metal basics
content.standfirst: The Black Sabbath guitarist’s first solo album in more than two decades pairs his heavy riffs with Norwegian singer Jørn Lande. Pitchfork’s review calls it Iommi’s strongest work under his own name.

sources.originalTitle: From the Dark

segments.body: On From the Dark, Tony Iommi returns to solo work with a heavy-metal record fronted by Norwegian vocalist Jørn Lande. The review hears a deliberate choice to avoid both a proposed final Black Sabbath album and the blues-rock direction of Iommi’s earlier collaborations with singer Glenn Hughes.

segments.title: A partnership built around the riffs
segments.body: The critic praises Iommi’s controlled, weighty guitar work and describes Lande’s performance as a career best, while noting that his admiration for Ronnie James Dio is audible. The review’s main reservation is Brian May’s guest solo on “Death Wake,” which it finds less distinctive than another lead from Iommi might have been.

content.headline: Elon Musk’s AI-made Odyssey is a hollow answer to Christopher Nolan’s film
content.shortHeadline: Musk’s AI-made Odyssey is a hollow answer to Nolan’s
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s review of Grok’s seven-minute Homer adaptation finds ponderous animation, flat performances and no real dramatic purpose. Its main value, the critic argues, is showing the gulf between generating images and making art.

image.caption: A still from the AI-generated Odyssey episode made with Grok.

sources.originalTitle: Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey review – the dullest, most pointless riposte possible to Christopher Nolan’s brilliant epic

segments.body: Elon Musk has released a seven-minute opening episode of an Odyssey made with Grok AI, after objecting online to Christopher Nolan’s version and claiming he could make a more authentic adaptation. The Guardian’s critic describes the result as an inert prologue, with computer-generated imagery and even-toned, robotic dialogue.

segments.title: A question of artistic value
segments.body: The review argues that the episode’s dramatic events—Odysseus leaving his family and joining the war, among them—feel motiveless, and that the work seems driven more by a wish to win an online argument than to tell Homer’s story. The critic allows that later episodes could improve, but says this first one highlights the difference between AI’s potential financial value and its artistic merit.

content.headline: We, the Hated captures the backlash and dilemmas of Just Stop Oil protests
content.shortHeadline: A documentary follows Just Stop Oil into hostile protests
content.standfirst: Rich Felgate’s film records activists facing abuse and violence while campaigning through disruptive direct action. The review sees the group’s purpose and the public’s anger, while questioning whether its tactics alienate the people it hopes to persuade.

image.caption: A scene from We, the Hated, filmed close to Just Stop Oil protests.

sources.originalTitle: We, the Hated review – standing up to be abused: behind the scenes with Just Stop Oil

segments.body: We, the Hated follows Just Stop Oil protests from close range, with director Rich Felgate filming among activists, including his girlfriend, Indigo Rumbelow. The footage shows road blockades, confrontations with drivers and arrests; the review describes verbal abuse and physical aggression directed at protesters.

segments.title: The cost of disruption
segments.body: The film gives activists space to argue that climate action cannot wait, while also showing hostile TV interviews and public frustration with tactics that inconvenience ordinary people. The critic says targeting infrastructure rather than the fossil-fuel industry can squander goodwill. Activists’ prison sentences and the campaign’s claimed political gains leave the film asking who bears responsibility for the conflict.

content.headline: City of Masks turns a West End theatre into a muddled ghost romance
content.shortHeadline: City of Masks is a muddled West End ghost story
content.standfirst: A young actor is coached by the ghost of a composer who died in the theatre where he is performing. The Guardian’s review likes Amanda Jiang’s mysterious presence but finds the film’s romance and plot increasingly baffling.

image.caption: Amanda Jiang as Eve in City of Masks.

sources.originalTitle: City of Masks review – theatreland ghost story with female phantom of the opera out for revenge

segments.body: In City of Masks, earnest actor Christian begins hearing the voice of Eve, a composer who died in a fire at the West End theatre now staging her musical. The film turns the Phantom of the Opera setup on its head, with a female ghost coaching a male performer as questions gather around the old fire.

segments.title: A haunted production
segments.body: The review praises Amanda Jiang’s sensual, mysterious performance as Eve but finds a clash between her style and the director character’s heightened intensity. As the suspected cause of the fire becomes part of the story and Christian develops feelings for Eve, the critic says the ghost-on-human romance grows uncomfortable and the plot harder to follow.

content.headline: You Can See Everything’s audience is still deciding what kind of film it is
content.shortHeadline: Audiences leave You Can See Everything unsure what to think
content.standfirst: At a sold-out New York screening, viewers laughed, murmured and sometimes fell silent during Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary. The Guardian finds that its unsettled audience response is part of the film’s growing appeal.

image.caption: Advertising for You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle America

segments.body: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s three-hour documentary You Can See Everything has become a substantial cinema hit. At a sold-out Times Square screening, the Guardian’s reporter watched a young audience respond with laughter, discomfort and uncertainty to a film that moves between the convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and the people around her.

segments.title: An audience in the mirror
segments.body: Viewers told the reporter that social-media clips and word of mouth had made the film feel like a cultural event, while many arrived without knowing its mid-film turn. Reactions ranged from sympathy for Holmes to suspicion of her account. The story asks whether this appetite signals audiences are ready for difficult cinema, or whether a documentary built around familiar TV figures gets more leeway than a conventional drama.

content.headline: Bad Day at the Office is a frantic first-person thriller that overstays its run
content.shortHeadline: Bad Day at the Office is a frantic thriller that wears you out
content.standfirst: John Hannah races through gangland London in a GoPro-shot action comedy full of parkour, absurd props and cartoonish violence. The Guardian enjoys its uninhibited energy but says the film’s 111 minutes outlast the novelty.

image.caption: John Hannah in Bad Day at the Office.

sources.originalTitle: Bad Day at the Office review – gratuitously entertaining Go-Pro thriller is like Crank meets The Hangover

segments.body: John Hannah plays Karl Davis, who wakes with amnesia in a trashed hotel room beside a dead body and soon finds himself dodging gangsters and fake police. Director Chee Keong Cheung shoots much of Bad Day at the Office from a first-person perspective, pushing the action through a hectic stream of parkour, fights and graphic on-screen annotations.

segments.title: Novelty at full speed
segments.body: The review calls the result “kind of glorious” in its delirious first stretch, as Karl scrambles across rooftops and fights his way through London’s underworld. But it finds that the gimmick loses force when the film returns to familiar revenge plotting, and argues that the relentless 111-minute pace makes the experience feel much longer.

content.headline: November’s film slate ranges from Ian Charleson’s Hamlet to Hunger Games
content.shortHeadline: November films: Ian Charleson’s Hamlet and a new Hunger Games
content.standfirst: The month’s cinema and streaming releases include Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson, another Hunger Games prequel and a new film from Ryusuke Hamaguchi. This guide gathers the titles and release dates to watch.

sources.originalTitle: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November

segments.body: November’s film releases range from Elsinore, in which Andrew Scott plays actor Ian Charleson as he takes on Hamlet while living with AIDS, to Sunrise on the Reaping, a new Hunger Games prequel. The guide also highlights Club Kid, a comedy-drama about a New York party promoter who meets the son he did not know he had.

segments.title: More to look out for
segments.body: The selection also includes Siân Heder’s disability-rights drama Being Heumann, a new film from Ryusuke Hamaguchi, and the animated fantasy Hexed. The guide provides cinema and streaming release dates across several territories, making it a useful browse for readers planning what to see next month.

content.headline: The Dropout is finding a new audience after You Can See Everything
content.shortHeadline: You Can See Everything is sending viewers back to The Dropout
content.standfirst: A new Elizabeth Holmes documentary has driven renewed interest in the 2022 TV drama and the podcast that preceded it. The Guardian argues that the older series still offers a bracing account of Theranos’s claims and their consequences.

image.caption: Amanda Seyfried and Naveen Andrews in The Dropout.

sources.originalTitle: Elizabeth Holmes mania: how the buzziest film of the year has resurrected a gut-twisting TV drama

segments.body: The success of You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, has sent viewers back to The Dropout. The Guardian reports that the Disney/Hulu series’ audience rose sharply after the film’s release, alongside a surge in listeners for the podcast of the same name.

segments.title: Beyond the spectacle
segments.body: The article contrasts the documentary’s open questions about Holmes’s self-presentation with The Dropout’s account of Theranos’s failed blood-testing claims, its workplace culture and the harm caused by unreliable results. Amanda Seyfried’s performance remains part of the series’ appeal, but the renewed attention also brings the company’s underlying facts back into view.

content.headline: The One About Matthew Perry makes a warm, unflinching tribute
content.shortHeadline: The One About Matthew Perry is a tender, candid tribute
content.standfirst: This three-part documentary draws on interviews with Perry’s family, friends and former partners to tell the story of his rise, addiction and death. The Guardian finds intimacy and generosity in a portrait that also speaks to those who loved him.

image.caption: Matthew Perry.

sources.originalTitle: The One About Matthew Perry review – the star of one of TV’s biggest ever shows gets a loving tribute

segments.body: The One About Matthew Perry follows the actor from his early years in Los Angeles to his fame on Friends and his death in 2023, aged 54. Family members, close friends and former partners describe him with evident affection, while the documentary does not sidestep the addiction that shaped his later life.

segments.title: A private grief, shared
segments.body: The review says the three-hour film is moving because its contributors speak about Perry as a person, not only as a star. Their memories of repeated attempts to get sober and the pain of watching him relapse lend the tribute a wider resonance for families affected by addiction, without turning the story into an easy or simple tragedy.

content.headline: Escaping Idi Amin recalls Asian Ugandans’ expulsion through survivors’ memories
content.shortHeadline: Escaping Idi Amin follows survivors of Uganda’s Asian expulsion
content.standfirst: Four people who were children in Uganda describe the violence and fear surrounding Idi Amin’s 1972 order that the country’s Asian population leave within 90 days. The Guardian finds their testimony an urgent account of displacement and refuge.

image.caption: A reconstruction of Harminder Singh and his father’s escape from Uganda to Britain.

sources.originalTitle: Escaping Idi Amin review – there’s a happy ending to this awful tale … and it should be a lesson to us all

segments.body: The two-part documentary Escaping Idi Amin hears from four people who grew up in Uganda and later became British citizens. They recall how the 1972 order forced around 80,000 Asian Ugandans to leave the country within 90 days, after Amin’s government had taken power and begun targeting its opponents.

segments.title: A question of refuge
segments.body: The review places the survivors’ memories alongside the hostility that greeted the prospect of their arrival in Britain, despite many holding British passports. It describes the family flight and the new lives they built after leaving Uganda, while arguing that the documentary’s account of scapegoating and asylum still has relevance beyond the events it records.

content.headline: Miranda Hart’s warmth becomes the heart of The Celebrity Traitors
content.shortHeadline: Miranda Hart brings warmth and laughter to The Celebrity Traitors
content.standfirst: The i Paper argues that Hart’s kindness, physical comedy and openness have become the standout qualities of this celebrity series. Her departure also prompted a rare moment of reflection on laughter, connection and returning to work after illness.

image.caption: Miranda Hart in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Miranda has brought wholesome joy back to TV

segments.body: The i Paper’s review of The Celebrity Traitors focuses on Miranda Hart, whose playful moments—from a mistaken “Big Mix” dance lesson to slapstick challenges—have become some of the series’ most widely shared scenes. The writer says Hart has brought a warmth to a programme otherwise built around suspicion, banishment and bluff.

segments.title: A return to the screen
segments.body: After her exit, Hart spoke about how the show let her reconnect with work and with other people after years of chronic fatigue syndrome. The review sees that candour as part of her comic appeal: she is willing to be vulnerable and not take herself too seriously, making the series’ language of laughter and connection feel more than a game.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans and the BBC waiting
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its latest run
content.standfirst: With no new Doctor announced, a planned Christmas special cancelled and the BBC’s Disney+ partnership ended, the series faces an uncertain pause. A reported history of its revivals shows why fans and industry observers disagree on what should come next.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since the 2025 series starring Ncuti Gatwa. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and put future production out to competitive tender, with no new Doctor announced. The corporation has declined interview requests, leaving questions about the show’s next chapter unanswered.

segments.title: A history of reinvention
segments.body: The feature traces how the series has repeatedly renewed itself, from its 2005 return after a 16-year break to successive changes of lead actor and showrunner. Some contributors blame weaker scripts and confusing storytelling for recent audience losses; others argue the show can recover if it returns to its core values and preserves the character’s established world. No single cause or solution is settled.

content.headline: Eight indie horror games offer everything from cursed cards to Antarctic penguin
content.shortHeadline: Eight indie horror games for Halloween, from penguins to devils
content.standfirst: A seasonal guide ranges across eerie adventures, occult card battles and low-budget interactive horror. Its picks include The Killing Stone, Silver Pines and Tenebris Somnia, alongside an Antarctic exploration game starring a penguin.

image.caption: A scene from The Killing Stone.

sources.originalTitle: Eight great new indie horror games for Halloween

segments.body: For Halloween, the Guardian rounds up eight independent horror releases, from an illustrated point-and-click fairy tale to Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival. The selection also includes a Scottish takeaway horror made with Gaelic dialogue and a 17th-century witch-hunt adventure, showing how broadly small-scale games are exploring the genre.

segments.title: Different kinds of fear
segments.body: Among the other picks are The Killing Stone, a card game set in a remote mansion, Silver Pines, a puzzle-filled mystery in an abandoned town, and Tenebris Somnia, which combines pixel art with live-action sequences. The guide also points readers towards Penguin Colony, an Antarctic exploration game in which a penguin observes Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure and cancelled Mass Effect leave fans mourning a lost RPG world
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans grieving a lost future
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s contributor reflects on EA’s announcement that the studio is closing and its planned Mass Effect game has been cancelled, with more than 400 jobs lost. The news lands particularly hard for players who found lasting meaning in the original trilogy.

image.caption: A scene from Mass Effect 3.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: EA has announced the closure of BioWare, cancelling its forthcoming Mass Effect game and putting more than 400 jobs at risk, according to the Guardian article. The writer, a games-industry veteran and long-time fan, describes the studio’s loss as a major blow to role-playing games and to players waiting for another story in the series.

segments.title: Why the trilogy endured
segments.body: The writer recalls how Mass Effect’s character relationships and consequential choices made a familiar mission to save the galaxy feel personal. Decisions carried across the trilogy, shaping the fate of characters and entire communities. That history helps explain the sense of loss, even as the article acknowledges BioWare’s recent struggles to produce a critical or commercial hit.

content.headline: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 balances explosive set pieces with character
content.shortHeadline: Modern Warfare 4 makes its battles serve the story
content.standfirst: A review praises the new campaign’s pace and spectacle, while a developer interview explains how Infinity Ward tried to make its missions and characters work together. The game’s political setting and its treatment of player choice remain part of the discussion.

image.caption: A scene from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

sources.originalTitle: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game
‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon

segments.body: The Guardian’s review calls Modern Warfare 4 a polished, fast-moving campaign, moving from parkour across Manhattan rooftops to a battle at a North Korean airbase. It also notes quieter sections and moments that force players into ethically stark actions, while criticising the ending for giving Captain Price’s story less weight than intended.

segments.title: Building action around people
segments.body: In a separate interview, narrative director Jeff Negus describes how Infinity Ward sought to make large-scale action matter by first establishing the people caught in it. The team used military and cultural consultants, including a dialect coach familiar with differences between North and South Korean speech, and tested and rearranged story beats during development.

content.headline: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort makes family gaming an easy group activity
content.shortHeadline: Switch Sports Resort is built for easy family fun
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s new collection adds seven activities to familiar sports, from archery and skateboarding to jetskiing. The Guardian’s reviewer finds it welcoming for children and adults, with a lively island setting that gives solo play more to explore.

image.caption: A scene from Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.

sources.originalTitle: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games

segments.body: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings back tennis, bowling and volleyball, adds golf and basketball, and introduces seven new activities including boxing, archery, skateboarding and jetskiing. The review finds most of them intuitive to pick up, with enough silliness to make the collection work well for family play.

segments.title: A place to return to
segments.body: The game’s island can be explored by jetski or plane, with beaches, stadiums and small details visible along the way. Unlockable outfits, sport variations and obstacle courses add reasons to keep playing outside the main events. The reviewer says the package became a fixture at home, sustaining both group sessions and a child’s interest over time.

content.headline: Personalised mRNA vaccine cuts melanoma recurrence risk in phase III trial
content.shortHeadline: Personalised mRNA vaccine cuts melanoma recurrence risk
content.standfirst: In a large trial, adding a patient-specific vaccine to pembrolizumab lowered the two-year risk of melanoma returning or death. The treatment still needs further study and regulatory review before routine use.

image.caption: Melanoma researcher Georgina Long, who described the trial findings as a major shift towards personalised cancer treatment.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Bespoke’ mRNA vaccine significantly reduces risk of melanoma recurrence or death, clinical trial shows

segments.body: The Australian-led phase III trial enrolled 1,137 people whose melanoma had been surgically removed but was considered at high risk of returning. Everyone received pembrolizumab; some also received intismeran, an mRNA vaccine designed around mutations in their own tumour. At two years, the combination group had a 42% lower risk of recurrence or death than the group receiving pembrolizumab alone.

segments.title: What remains to be established
segments.body: After two years, 82% of those given the combination were alive and free of recurrence, compared with 70% of those treated with pembrolizumab alone. Researchers say longer follow-up is needed to assess survival and how durable the benefit will be. The vaccine is not yet a standard treatment and may not help everyone; further study and regulatory review are still required.

content.headline: Optogenetic treatment restores useful vision in six of 10 patients
content.shortHeadline: Light-based gene therapy restores some vision in six patients
content.standfirst: A small trial used gene therapy to make retinal cells respond to amber light, helping some people with advanced retinitis pigmentosa perform simple tasks. The approach is experimental and does not restore normal sight.

image.caption: Optogenetics uses light to control nerve-cell activity.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: Optogenetics uses light to switch nerve cells on or off. In a study of 10 people with severe sight loss from retinitis pigmentosa, researchers delivered a gene to the retina so some cells would respond to amber light; patients wore special glasses that converted ordinary light. After three months, six participants had improved enough to complete tasks such as picking up a cup.

segments.title: A limited, early result
segments.body: The treatment did not restore normal vision. Participants first perceived dots of light and had to learn to interpret them; they could not distinguish faces. Researchers are working on approaches that might provide more detail. Optogenetics is also being explored for conditions including pain, epilepsy and deafness, but those applications remain at earlier stages and some would require gene therapy that may be irreversible.

content.headline: Scientists recreate the colour-changing effect of ancient Roman glass
content.shortHeadline: Scientists recreate Roman glass that changes colour in light
content.standfirst: Researchers at the University of Sheffield have reproduced the green-to-red optical effect of the fourth-century Lycurgus Cup using gold and silver nanoparticles. The work may help explain how Roman glassmakers achieved the striking colours.

image.caption: The Lycurgus Cup appears green in ordinary light and red when lit from behind.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s magic’: scientists rediscover how to make ancient Roman colour-changing glass

segments.body: The Lycurgus Cup appears jade green in ordinary light and ruby red when illuminated from behind. Researchers at the University of Sheffield have replicated the effect using an ancient recipe derived from a fragment of Roman glass, embedding tiny gold and silver nanocrystals in glass as it cooled.

segments.title: How the effect works
segments.body: The nanoparticles interact with light in different ways: light passing through the glass is filtered so reds and oranges show through, while light reflected from its surface is scattered to produce an opaque green. Archaeological materials expert Ian Freestone said the Sheffield work comes closer to the original colours than a previous 1960s replica. He noted that furnace conditions could have made the effect difficult for Roman craftspeople to control.

content.headline: A fertile Cavendish banana opens a new route to disease-resistant fruit
content.shortHeadline: Fertile Cavendish banana may open a route to disease resistance
content.standfirst: A research partnership says it has developed a fertile Cavendish line, potentially making cross-breeding possible for the usually sterile fruit. The details remain undisclosed, and any new variety would still need to meet growers’ tests for taste, yield and disease resistance.

image.caption: A researcher works on the banana-breeding programme aimed at tackling crop disease.

sources.originalTitle: Have scientists finally found a way to save the banana from disaster?

segments.body: Most commercial Cavendish bananas are grown from offshoots and are nearly genetically identical, leaving crops vulnerable to diseases such as Tropical Race 4. Yelloway, a collaboration between Chiquita and crop-improvement company KeyGene, says it has developed a fully fertile Cavendish line, which could allow breeders to cross it with other bananas.

segments.title: A possible route, not a finished solution
segments.body: Yelloway has not disclosed how the line was produced or how many chromosomes it has. Researchers say crossing it with disease-resistant bananas could yield useful offspring, but the fruit might differ substantially from Cavendish. Any candidate would still need to resist disease, produce high yields and taste acceptable. Other approaches include gene editing and a genetically modified Cavendish already approved for consumption in Australia and New Zealand.

content.headline: Climate change is prompting research into new crops for British farms
content.shortHeadline: New crops could help British farms adapt to hotter, drier summers
content.standfirst: Researchers are testing drought-tolerant crops such as lupins and chickpeas as heat and dry conditions affect familiar harvests. Their suitability for British farming still needs to be tested across varieties, locations and seasons.

image.caption: A lupin bhaji made with a crop researchers are exploring for warmer, drier conditions.

sources.originalTitle: The protein-packed superfoods of the future – that you could grow in your garden

segments.body: This year’s hot, dry summer harmed yields of crops including wheat, barley, broccoli, peas and potatoes, according to the reporting. Researchers at Southampton University are working with farmers, food companies and chefs to investigate alternatives that might suit a warmer, drier Britain, including lupins and chickpeas.
